messages.author: e19ea506112fd25b
messages.subject: scaling parameters & divergent transitions
parts:
Hi,

Based on stan expert opinion scaling parameters is quite important to improve numerical stability. However so far I didn't find any guidelines - is it better to divide parameter by some constant or take log or some other tricks. I wish there was some discussion in the manual or github. For example, the approximated posterior in unscaled parameter space looks like:
theta4 ~ lognormal(-7.87,0.99)
theta7 ~ lognormal(12.55,0.91)
Does it make sense to work in the parameter space of scaled_theta4=exp(theta4) and scaled_theta7=log(theta7) or is it better to define scaled_theta4=theta4*0.0006 where 0.0006=mean(rlnorm(10000,-7.87,0.99) and scaled_theta7=theta7/400000 where 40000=mean(rlnorm(10000,12.55,0.91))?

Experts tell us that divergent transitions may lead to bias (there is a lot in this list) but it is hard to mine this info and glue together to get a good guidance. I wonder if scaling parameters has anything to do with divergent transitions. It would be great to summarize this info similar to https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations.

The model I am working with is a PBPK model defined as a system of ODEs. Solving ODEs has some tolerances associated with it. In a PBPK model material balances have to be conserved (in=out) however because of ODE solver the material balances range in -10-3 to 10-3. May this be a cause for divergent transitions?

Thanks for any insight,
Linas

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] scaling parameters & divergent transitions
parts:
It's all about the unconstrained scale. The closer
you can get to zero mean and unit covariance multinormal,
the better.

If there's too much correlation or varying curvature,
reparameterization can help. See the chapter in the manual
and the Betancourt/Girolami paper on hierarchical models.

Yes, performance will be sensitive to the tolerance of the ODEs.
We're not even sure if this is model dependent. There are
absolute and relative tolerances.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] scaling parameters & divergent transitions
parts:
Hi,
this is something I am also struggling with. There is a lot of talk on non-centered parametrizations, but as far as I understand, this means making sure that _prior_ distribution is zero mean, unit covariance multinomial. 
I think the question is: does it make sense to reparametrize according to the sensitivity of the log posterior to small changes in the parameters?

So for example:
if we have parameters:
alpha ~ normal(0,1)
beta ~ normal(0,1)

and data model
y ~ normal(2^alpha + beta, 1)

the prior is zero mean, unit covariance, but a small change in alpha will affect the posterior much more than a small change in beta. To my intuition this sounds like a typical "uneven curvature"

If this is the case, does it make sense to reparametrize to gamma = 2^alpha? This would give
log2(gamma) ~ normal(0,1)
beta ~ normal(0,1)

y ~ normal(gamma + beta, 1)

the paremetrization (gamma, beta) des not have zero mean, unit covariance, but the curvature of the log posterior should (in my intuition) be more even in all places and directions.

Thanks for any clarifications
Martin

As I understand the current state of the art is partially centered parametrization. Centered - lots of data, non-centered - little data, partially centered - middle ground. While there are theoretical papers it would be nice to describe how to use this in the stan domain. I recently enjoyed reading the case study on divergent transitions for 8 schools example but still feel the gap how to apply this knowledge to the problem at hand. It would be nice to have some guidelines how to reparametrize based on the curvature of pair plots.

Linas

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] scaling parameters & divergent transitions
parts:
You have to look at what's happening on the unconstrained
scale. That's where Stan's actually sampling.

I don't think it's so much sensitivity to parameters as you
want the unconstrained parameters to be relatively freely
moving between -2 and 2 and not allowed to get huge and
not constrained to stay small. Then the initial mass matrix
guess will be right and everything will move well.

The best you can do is look at the pairs (or triples in
ShinyStan) plots to see what's happening to groups of
parameters.

By varying curvature in the posterior, we mean that the Hessian
(second derivative matrix) changes as the parameters change.
That's the hierarchical modeling case that the non-centered
parameterization avoids (see the manual chapter on reparameterization
and the funnel example for an extreme case).

Linas --- I don't know what the partially centered parameterization
is. Did someone write that up somewhere?

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] scaling parameters & divergent transitions
parts:
There do exist continuous interpolations between centered and
non-centered distributions, but it turns out that the transition to
optimally centered and optimally non-centered happens so quickly
that in practice none of them are all that useful.  

The general issue here is that because you can build a arbitrary
model in the Stan language it can have arbitrary pathologies and
there will be no general solution to sampling problems.  We have
worked to develop as many broad techniques as possible, but
that’s all we can do without interrogating the exact model.

At that most general level diverges occur when the posterior
on the unconstrained scaled features strong curvature.  This
is straightforward to identify by running many iterations and
looking at the sampled that diverged and those that didn’t to
hunt down the source of the problem, which can then inform
what in your model is ultimately being problematic and what
you might want to adjust.  If you are using many constrained
types then you’ll want to use the diagnostic file which outputs
the unconstrained parameters, although it may not be as easy
to use in some of the interfaces.
On Apr 10, 2017, at 12:35 PM, Linas Mockus <linasm...@gmail.com> wrote:

Bob,

I swear I saw some discussion by Michael about him using partially centered parametrizations but can't find it now. However, there is a paper "A General Framework for the Parametrization of Hierarchical Models" which gives some idea.

Linas

Yes, I agree that being general precludes very detailed recipes. I found case studies very helpful. And perhaps adding couple of more studies where divergent transitions drive re-parametrization would be awesome. Since I am planning to contribute my 6+ month stan project maybe this could be such a study. One confounding factor is that my model is a bunch of ODEs and the accuracy of ODE solution may affect the divergencies.

Per Bob's advice I have scaled all my parameters to unit normal (single variate since parameters seems to be independent based on pairs plot). 
stheta~N(0,1). The parameters passed to ODE solver are transformed parameters in the form: theta=exp(a+b*stheta). To represent individual parameters I used non-centered parametrization, i.e. theta_ind=theta*exp(u*sigma_ind) where u~N(0,1). I have used exponential form since physiological parameters are positive and presumably log normal. Then after plotting pairs plot I saw the dreaded shape of a funnel and it seems bunch of diverged (in red) were at the neck of the funnel while some others looked random. I am simply stuck with any ideas for further reparametrization since I am already using non-centered. For some pairs (theta,sigma_ind) divergencies were on the side. The model is attached.

parts:
I am using cmdstan so I guess all messages go to redirected output.

It is funny, after parametrizing in unit scale stheta~N(0,1) I saw only
one divergence in four chains. The computational time substantially
increased since I am using transformed parameters theta=exp(a+b*stheta).
Simulation now takes two days instead of one, it is half way done. Will
let you know after simulation completes but maybe your advice is the
right reparametrization!!!

Now what bugs me is a poor fit (see my latest question). Since one
dataset has a single point per individual while other one has a dozen
data points per individual the fit for the first data set is very poor.
I wonder how to increase the weight of observations in the first data
set. Maybe artificially replicate the points for each individual by
adding some small noise?

Linas

messages.author: e19ea506112fd25b
messages.subject: Re[3]: [stan-users] scaling parameters & divergent transitions
parts:
I had 4 chains with 200 warmups and 1000 iterations each. Only 2 chains
indicated a single divergence. Looks like that your proposed
parametrization magically removes divergencies.

However I have a question. In this parametrization of unit scaled
natural parameters I saw strong correlation between two parameters.
Let's say parameters a and b are strongly correlated. My initial
parametrization was using parameters a0=a/b and b0=b which showed no
correlation between a0&b0 but may have lead to divergencies. My question
is if this observation makes sense/may it lead to divergencies/should I
use chol to remove the correlation?

The second observation was more specific to the model. There is so
called MM equation which defines nolinear elimination of drug. It has
two parameters - Vmax maximum rate achieved by the system at saturating
substrate concentration Km. My initial parametrization was theta1=Km and
theta2=Vmax/Km so theta1&theta2 looked independent. After I switched to
Vmax & Km parametrization the pairs shape became funny - it seems
somebody cut out the part of the circle (see attached). Is this
something to worry about? stheta2 is Vmax scaled to unit and stheta2 is
Km scaled to unit. Scaling was reversed engineered - from Vmax posterior
I have identified scaling factors s1&s2 so that Vmax=exp(s1+s2*stheta1)
where stheta1~N(0,1). It was a weird way but seems it worked. I wonder
if there is a more straightforward/robust way.

Linas
